mcqs.question: An application needs to send a 4000-byte message over standard Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU. What has to happen?
options: Nothing — Ethernet frames can hold any payload size, MTU is just a recommendation
The switch automatically compresses the payload to fit under 1500 bytes
The 4000-byte message gets fragmented into multiple IP packets, each small enough to fit within the 1500-byte Ethernet payload limit
The message is dropped, since Ethernet cannot carry messages larger than one frame
mcqs.explanation: MTU is a hard cap on frame payload, so a message larger than it must be split into multiple smaller IP packets (fragmentation) each carried in its own frame. MTU is enforced, not a suggestion (the recommendation-only claim is false); switches don't compress payloads (the switch-compression claim); and the message isn't simply dropped — it's fragmented instead (the dropped-message claim is false).

mcqs.question: On a legacy shared-medium Ethernet segment, two devices transmit at the exact same instant. What does CSMA/CD do next?
options: The switch buffers both frames and forwards them sequentially
The collision is silently ignored since Ethernet has no mechanism to detect it
The device with the lower MAC address automatically gets priority and retransmits immediately
Both devices detect the resulting collision, stop transmitting, and each waits a random backoff period before retrying
mcqs.explanation: Collision detection plus random backoff is exactly CSMA/CD's mechanism — both senders back off with independently randomized delays so they don't collide again immediately. There's no switch involved on a shared segment by definition (the switch-buffering claim), no MAC-address priority scheme (the MAC-priority claim), and collisions are explicitly detected, not ignored (the collision-ignored claim).

mcqs.question: A company wants Finance and Engineering on the same physical switches but wants a broadcast from a Finance PC to never reach an Engineering PC. What solves this without buying separate switches?
options: 802.1Q VLAN tagging, splitting the switch into logically separate broadcast domains
Using CSMA/CD to filter which devices receive broadcasts
Assigning Finance devices MAC addresses from a different OUI range
Increasing the Ethernet MTU for Finance devices only
mcqs.explanation: VLAN tagging is precisely designed for this — logically separating broadcast domains on shared physical switch hardware. CSMA/CD deals with collision avoidance, not broadcast scoping; OUI ranges only indicate manufacturer and have no isolation effect; and MTU size has nothing to do with broadcast domain separation.

mcqs.question: Why can't a router simply forward a packet to a destination's MAC address across the internet instead of using an IP address?
options: MAC addresses are too short to represent internet-scale destinations
MAC addresses are flat, vendor-assigned identifiers with no hierarchical structure tied to network location, so there's no way to aggregate them into scalable routing table entries
MAC addresses change every time a device reboots, making them unreliable for routing
Routers are physically incapable of reading MAC address fields
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is structure: IP addresses are allocated in hierarchical, aggregatable blocks that let routing tables stay small and scalable; MAC addresses are flat and vendor-assigned with zero relationship to network topology. Address length isn't the limiting factor (the too-short claim), MAC addresses are typically stable and burned-in (the reboot-changes-MAC claim is false), and routers absolutely read MAC fields — for the local hop, not global routing (the claim that routers can't read MAC fields is false).
